                    ### Question
                    A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a knife wound to his back. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Examination shows a 5-cm deep stab wound at the level of T9. He withdraws the right foot to pain but is unable to sense vibration or whether his right toe is flexed or extended. Sensation in the left leg is normal. Motor strength is 5/5 in all extremities. Rectal tone is normal. Which of the following spinal column structures was most likely affected?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Dorsal root
opb. Posterior spinal artery
opc. Central spinal cord grey matter
opd. Lateral corticospinal tract
ope. Artery of Adamkiewicz

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The knife wound at T9 likely affected the dorsal columns, which are responsible for proprioception and vibration sense. The patient's inability to sense vibration or determine the position of his right toe indicates damage to the sensory pathways that carry these modalities, specifically the dorsal columns. The dorsal root is involved in transmitting sensory information from the periphery to the spinal cord, but the specific loss of proprioception and vibration suggests that the dorsal columns (part of the posterior funiculus) were affected rather than the dorsal root itself. Therefore, the most likely structure affected is the dorsal columns, which are part of the posterior root of the spinal nerve. The preserved motor strength and intact withdrawal reflex indicate that the lateral corticospinal tract and other motor pathways remain intact. Thus, the correct answer is that the dorsal columns were affected, aligning with the consensus on sensory pathway functions.
